a_rows_sample.anchor: Clarify(Q,K,C) \rightarrow Q'
a_rows_sample.statement: Introduces an explicit Clarification operation: Intent(Q) yields either CandidateIntent (if sufficiently interpretable) or ClarificationRequired (if underdetermined); Clarify(Q,K,C) -> Q' lets Sārathi ask 'What do you mean by those?' instead of hallucinating a dimension model. New major invariant: InsufficientSemanticDetermination ⇏ Assumption.

a_rows_sample.anchor: InsufficientSemanticDetermination \not\Rightarrow Assumption
a_rows_sample.statement: Validates the proposed Clarification concept: Arjuna explicitly asks Krishna to determine which teaching is beneficial rather than silently assuming, matching Question -> Clarification -> BetterProblemDefinition; recommended to become a fundamental KnowledgeOS rule.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Interpretation \rightarrow CandidateDimensions \rightarrow GapDetection \rightarrow Clarification
a_rows_sample.statement: Applies the closed pipeline to the incomplete-question problem: Arjuna's 'show me those with whom I have to fight' yields Source Observation 'Arjuna asked...', Semantic Interpretation {Actor=Arjuna, Action=fight, Target=unknown, Relationship=with, Modality=obligation}, then KnowledgeOS discovers Missing={Side,Identity,Relationship,Context} and does NOT answer prematurely, following Interpretation->CandidateDimensions->GapDetection->Clarification. Proposes stress-testing the frozen model against eight cases (DB result, unstructured document, Internet page, human statement, LLM answer, conflicting sources, incomplete question, source that later becomes stale) before declaring the Observation boundary computationally closed.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Case 7: Incomplete Question ... The model stops at interpretation and does not prematurely assert knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: Runs the closed model against all eight previously-proposed test cases with full worked traces, every verdict 'Clean': (1) DB result — high trust, Strong support; (2) unstructured document — Moderate support, Stale validity flagged from an outdated date reference; (3) internet page from an unknown site — Weak support, High uncertainty; (4) human belief statement — Reported acquisition, captures 'belief' as part of the semantic structure separate from the fact claim; (5) LLM answer — AI_Generated acquisition, None support, VeryHigh uncertainty, 'correctly marks LLM output as low-trust'; (6) conflicting DB vs LLM sources — produces a relational Conflict object (type Logical, status Active); (7) incomplete question (Arjuna's 'those with whom I have to fight') — CandidateAssertion is explicitly None since target is unknown, triggering GapDetection(MissingTarget, severity High) and a Clarification request instead of a premature assertion; (8) stale source — a 2025 observation's validity is updated to Stale when a 2026 observation supersedes it, without losing history. Declares: 'The Observation boundary is computationally closed', with final invariants Artifact≠SourceObservation≠SemanticInterpretation≠CandidateAssertion≠Assertion, and 'every Assertion must trace back to at least one SourceObservation through its lineage.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: An observation is a purpose-driven act of attending to a portion of reality, producing a structured representation of selected dimensions, at a specific point in time, by a specific observer.
b_rows_sample.statement: Observation is formally defined as O = (X_t, P, A, C, tau, S) with Reality/target X_t, Purpose P, Observer/Access A, Context C, Time tau, and Selection S; Observation != Reality, and Observation is observer-, purpose-, and time-dependent.

type_signature.domain: Reality x Purpose x Observer x Context x Time

b_rows_sample.anchor: I would not yet accept the statement “observation is always purpose-driven” as a universal axiom. We should test that through the Gita and the lenses first.
b_rows_sample.statement: A reviewer refuses to freeze 'observation is always purpose-driven' as a universal axiom, deferring it to later Gita/lens testing rather than accepting it as given.

b_rows_sample.anchor: I would distinguish the thing being observed from the act/process of observing and from the resulting representation... R_t = Reality at time t ... Obs = Observation Act ... O = Observation Result
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the initial O tuple by separating Reality (R_t), the Observation Act (Obs), and the Observation Result (O_t), and further renames the observed target from 'Reality X_t' to 'Target of Observation T_t' with Reality superset-of T_t, to avoid equating the observed target with the whole of reality.

b_rows_sample.anchor: I would also separate Observer from Access ... A_o=Observer ... A_c=Access Condition ... The same observer can have different access conditions.
b_rows_sample.statement: Splits the combined 'Observer/Access' element A into Observer (A_o) and Access Condition (A_c), noting the same observer can have different access conditions (e.g. production read access vs no network-device access), anticipating this will matter for modelling Sanjaya.

b_rows_sample.anchor: I would also question whether Selection is an independent primitive ... S=f(P,A_c,C,M) ... We shouldn't decide this yet.
b_rows_sample.statement: Leaves open whether Selection S is a primitive of observation or is mathematically derived from Purpose, Access, Context and Method (S=f(P,A_c,C,M)).

b_rows_sample.anchor: an observation can contain raw or partially processed evidence that has not yet become knowledge ... Observation -> ObservationRepresentation -> Knowledge
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues Observation does not directly equal Knowledge; inserts an intermediate ObservationRepresentation stage, illustrated by the layered example Observation('Port 8081 responded') vs Knowledge('Nexus service is reachable') vs Interpretation vs Guidance as four distinct epistemic objects.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Arjuna sees the battlefield. But what does he actually know? ... Observation -> Meaning -> Conflict rather than Observation -> CorrectUnderstanding
b_rows_sample.statement: Uses Gita chapter 1 (Arjuna seeing the battlefield) as an early test case supporting Observation != Knowledge and even Observation != Understanding, since his observation produces conflict/meaning rather than correct understanding.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Observation = Projection_{S_O}(Reality) ... S_O is not necessarily the set of all dimensions that exist.
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes Observation as a projection of Reality onto a selected dimension subspace S_O of a potentially infinite dimension space D (S_O subset-of D, S_O != D in general): Observation = Projection_{S_O}(Reality).

b_rows_sample.anchor: The dimension d_101 did not necessarily come into existence Tuesday. It was already a possible dimension of the target state. What changed was: KnowledgeOS/Knower's representation
b_rows_sample.statement: Uses a 'Monday selection of 100 dimensions, Tuesday adds dimension d_101' example to argue that a newly noticed dimension need not be newly existing -- what changes is the observer's/KnowledgeOS's representation, not the underlying possible-dimension space.

b_rows_sample.anchor: ObsAct=(T,P,A_o,A_c,C,\tau,S,M) ... O=Observe(ObsAct) ... K=Interpret/Assert(O)
b_rows_sample.statement: Converges on a revised eight-element Observation Act tuple ObsAct=(Target,Purpose,Observer,AccessCondition,Context,Time,Selection,Method), with O=Observe(ObsAct) and a separate epistemic transformation K=Interpret/Assert(O).

b_rows_sample.anchor: O_t = (X_t, P, A, C, \tau, S) ... Purpose (P) = "Should I participate in this battle?"
b_rows_sample.statement: Instantiates every element of the Observation tuple for Arjuna: X_t=Kuruksetra battlefield, P='Should I participate in this battle?', A=Arjuna (kshatriya, direct participant), C=family war/moral dilemma, tau=moment before battle, S={relatives, teachers, friends, kinsmen}.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Arjuna is not an external, detached observer. He is inside the observation, which profoundly affects what he sees and how he interprets it.
b_rows_sample.statement: Argues the observer can be inside the observed reality (a direct participant/knower+actor), which affects the resulting observation and interpretation -- a case the abstract O=(X,P,A,C,tau,S) model must accommodate.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge Increased \not\Rightarrow Uncertainty Decreased ... K_{t+1} > K_t \quad \text{but} \quad U_{dec}(K_{t+1}) > U_{dec}(K_t)
b_rows_sample.statement: Key finding: Arjuna's increased knowledge after observation does not reduce his decision uncertainty -- it increases it; knowledge increasing does not imply decision uncertainty decreasing.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Krishna is not observing the battlefield for himself. He is observing Arjuna's observation and understanding ... O_2 = Krishna -> Arjuna's Epistemic State
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes second-order observation: while Arjuna performs first-order observation of the battlefield (O_1), Krishna/KnowledgeOS-Sarathi can perform a second-order observation of the Knower's epistemic state itself (O_2 = Observe(KnowerState)) -- what the Knower knows, doesn't know, believes, is uncertain about, and what decision state they are in.

b_rows_sample.anchor: P_O = purpose of observation ... P_D = purpose of decision ... P_O \neq P_D at least potentially. He initially wants to see. That seeing subsequently creates a deeper decision problem.
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the earlier framing of Arjuna's purpose ('should I fight?') by separating the purpose of observation (P_O: wanting to see who he must contend with) from the purpose of decision (P_D: whether to fight), arguing observation does not necessarily begin with a fully formulated question.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We should not use > until we define an ordering on knowledge. Instead: KnowledgeExtent(K_{t+1}) > KnowledgeExtent(K_t)
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the informal inequality K_{t+1} > K_t (no ordering on knowledge yet defined) to the more careful KnowledgeExtent(K_{t+1}) > KnowledgeExtent(K_t), while DecisionUncertainty(K_{t+1}) > DecisionUncertainty(K_t) may simultaneously hold.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The current Observation definition contains O=(X,P,A,C,\tau,S) where S is Selection. But later we use S for Statement. That is a mathematical notation collision.
b_rows_sample.statement: Flags a notation collision between Observation's Selection component S and Statement S, recommending renaming Observation's selection component (e.g. to Sel or Sigma_O) and reserving S strictly for Statement going forward.

b_rows_sample.anchor: O = \Pi_{P,A,C,\tau}(\Omega) ... where \Pi selects or reconstructs the portion relevant to the observation.
b_rows_sample.statement: Reformulates Observation as a projection/reconstruction operator over a (potentially infinite) reality space Omega rather than a subset: O=Pi_{P,A,C,tau}(Omega), motivated by the infinite-knowledge-space hypothesis that an observation need not be a literal subset of reality.

b_rows_sample.anchor: X_t \rightarrow O_t \rightarrow R_t \rightarrow A_t \rightarrow K_t
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the too-simple Reality->Observation->Knowledge pipeline into X_t (domain/reality) -> O_t (observation) -> R_t (semantic reconstruction/interpretation) -> A_t (assertion) -> K_t (knowledge state), with the critical point Observation ≠ Interpretation ≠ Assertion ≠ Knowledge, illustrated with the Bhīṣma example (seeing him = observation; 'Bhīṣma is a person' = interpretation; 'Bhīṣma is Arjuna's grandfather' = assertion; the same claim with provenance and epistemic qualification = knowledge).

b_rows_sample.anchor: O = (Subject,\ Payload,\ Source,\ Time,\ Context,\ Provenance)
b_rows_sample.statement: Formal definition of Observation as a tuple (Subject, Payload, Source, Time, Context, Provenance), answering who/what observed, what, when, in what context, through what mechanism, with what provenance; and the invariant Observed(x) ⇏ True(x) — an observation is not automatically true.

group_evidence.why_grouped: labels co-occur in the same contribution's labels[] 2 separate times across the corpus

a_rows_sample.anchor: Vedic texts: Field, discrimination, transformation, persistent knower. Birkenbihl: Knowledge network / association. Maltz: Goal-directed cybernetic feedback. Pearl: Causal graph / explanation. ... We don't ask: Which author is correct about KnowledgeOS? We ask: What different intellectual lenses exp
a_rows_sample.statement: Assembles a 10-row comparative table of external metaphorical lenses (Vedic texts, Birkenbihl, Maltz, Pearl, Dretske, Davidson, Bayesian epistemology, Kalman filtering, Hilbert space, Zero Lens) each mapped to a possible metaphor, restating the governing methodological question as 'what different intellectual lenses expose aspects of the same underlying engineering problem?' rather than 'which author is correct about KnowledgeOS?', with resulting propositions to be tested independently of source authority.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Eileen Cornell Way -- Knowledge Representation and Metaphor: Representation itself is metaphorical/constructive ... 5 stars. Judea Pearl & Dana Mackenzie -- The Book of Why: Causal graph as a landscape for asking 'why?' ... 5 stars. Birkenbihl 4 stars. Hofstadter -- I Am a Strange Loop 4 stars. Glei
b_rows_sample.statement: Ranks six candidate books as metaphorical lenses for KnowledgeOS with assigned strength ratings: Way's Knowledge Representation and Metaphor (5 stars, representation is itself metaphorical/constructive), Pearl & Mackenzie's The Book of Why (5 stars, causal graph as explanation landscape), Birkenbihl's Stroh im Kopf? (4 stars, knowledge as associative network), Hofstadter's I Am a Strange Loop (4 stars, self-reference/recursive identity), Gleick's The Information (4 stars, information as structure/transmission/transformation), and Calvino's Invisible Cities (4 stars, multiple perspectives on one reality); explicitly states the first two are particularly relevant to where KnowledgeOS currently stands.

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'comparative-lens-landscape-table' POSSIBLY relates to 'six-candidate-books-ranked' (batch B0067). Note: A 10-source comparative table of external metaphorical lenses for KnowledgeOS, overlapping with but broader than the six-book survey in S2815.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K = S + iA where S = semantic state, A = authority state ... What something says and whether the organization is authorized to treat it as true are different dimensions.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes representing a knowledge artifact's semantic-state and authority-state as the real and imaginary components of a complex number, so the two dimensions are never collapsed into a single scalar.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ΔK = ΔS + iΔA ... They disagree semantically. from: They agree semantically, but their authority states conflict. Those are completely different governance problems.
a_rows_sample.statement: Extends the complex-number model with a difference operator separating semantic conflict from authority conflict as two distinct governance problems, noting compatibility with the existing R-CONFLICT concept.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Do not make 'complex number = knowledge' ... KnowledgeOS is fundamentally about: meaning, evidence, provenance, authority, lifecycle, invariants, relationships, decisions, governance. A complex number cannot represent all of that.
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicitly warns against equating knowledge itself with a complex number; mathematics is proposed as a domain-supporting analytical mechanism layered above the domain model, never the domain model itself.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K = [S, E, A, P, T]^T ... complex numbers become a special two-dimensional projection: z = S+iA or z = E+iP.
a_rows_sample.statement: Generalizes the two-dimensional complex-number model into a five-dimensional vector (semantic validity, evidence strength, authority, provenance integrity, temporal validity), with any complex-number model recast as a special two-axis projection of the fuller vector.

a_rows_sample.anchor: EKS PKS AIP → Current architecture → Domain discovery → Invariants → Knowledge concepts → Mathematical properties → Mathematical representation. Not: Complex numbers → invent KnowledgeOS model.
a_rows_sample.statement: States a DDD-priority ordering rule: mathematical representation must be derived last, after current-architecture evidence, domain discovery, invariants, and knowledge concepts are established — never chosen first and used to invent the domain model.

a_rows_sample.anchor: I would record this as a research hypothesis, not an architecture decision ... Can the semantic state and authority state of real EKS/PKS artifacts be represented without losing domain meaning? If yes, investigate further. If no, discard the model.
a_rows_sample.statement: Proposes the first concrete falsifiable experiment for the complex-number model: test K=S+iA against real EKS/PKS artifacts and discard the model if domain meaning is lost.

a_rows_sample.anchor: CAPPI's numeric epistemic stack (mu/tau/w -> Bayesian fusion -> quality score) has ZERO current-architecture support. None of EKS/PKS/AIP uses a continuous calibrated confidence signal, a Bayesian fusion step, or a scalar quality score.
a_rows_sample.statement: Reports the single strongest case in the investigation of an elegant external principle unsupported by current evidence: continuous calibrated confidence, per-instance uncertainty, and a reliability weight (mu/tau/w) are absent from all three baselines, whose discrete verdict vocabularies and honest UNKNOWN answers are philosophically the inverse of a probabilistic quality score.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ALT-09 · Complex-number epistemic model
a_rows_sample.statement: K(t) = M(t) + iA(t) — knowledge as a complex quantity over time (20260821-2325, root era) — was a modeling-tool exploration never carried into kernel or Step eras; the notation K_t was later re-coined with a different meaning; no v0.2 correspondence, and the same-notation collision was recorded in the GN-28 delta pass.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 11 · ADDENDUM (GN-28 delta pass, 2026-08-28) — KnowledgeState/K_t, three senses
a_rows_sample.statement: KnowledgeState/K_t has three senses, two predating the formal model: (a) engineering sense, 20260820-231930 (event-driven architecture, a state in an event flow paired with an Outbox record); (b) complex-number epistemic model, 20260821-2325, K(t) = M(t) + iA(t) — same notation as the later formal K_t, entirely different model, registered as ALT-09; (c) the formal K_t of the Step era. 228/233 carrier files respectively; the formal sense dominates by volume but is the youngest.

a_rows_sample.anchor: FA-delta-8 · K_t naming register (three senses)
a_rows_sample.statement: Adds a K_t naming register for its three historically-distinct senses, graded [RC], grounded in concept-evolution section 11 and ALT-09.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_t / KnowledgeState row
a_rows_sample.statement: K_t/KnowledgeState: L2 sense is state over 8 primitives; repository (L3) sense is event-flow state; historical sense is the complex-number model K(t)=M(t)+iA(t) (ALT-09); reconciliation D-FA-6: qualified naming.

a_rows_sample.anchor: D-FA-6 K_t names evidence chain
a_rows_sample.statement: D-FA-6 (K_t names) evidence chain: ALT-09 / concept-evolution section 11 [E/H].

a_rows_sample.anchor: D-FA-6 · Naming-collision register extended to K_t
a_rows_sample.statement: Decision: K_t unqualified is the L2 formal knowledge state; K(t)=M(t)+iA(t) is [H] (ALT-09); event-flow 'Knowledge State' is L3/engineering usage — same policy as D-FA-3. Needs ratification: YES (same terminology policy).

a_rows_sample.anchor: 4 · Terminology register — collisions bound (D-FA-3, D-FA-6)
a_rows_sample.statement: 'Zero' unqualified = Zero(K,EC) (L2); the boundary meta-principle is referred to as Z-KOS-001 (L1/L3); the absence-lens sense is [H]. Same rule for K_t (L2 formal state; the complex-number K(t)=M(t)+iA(t) is [H]/ALT-09; the event-flow 'Knowledge State' is an L3/engineering usage). Naming similarity is never semantic identity [R — GN-29 rule 6].

a_rows_sample.anchor: 7 · Terminology rules (binding, from FA-4)
a_rows_sample.statement: Binds book-wide terminology: unqualified 'Zero' = Zero(K,EC) only, the meta-principle is always 'Z-KOS-001', absence-lens Zero appears only in Part I with dates; K_t unqualified = the formal state, ALT-09 and engineering usage always qualified; 'Lord' appears only as documented history; 'Committed' only in the A6 decision-boundary sense; Sanskrit terms carry their lens origin on first use; a terminology conformance table ships with every chapter's claims.md.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 1 · The binding register
a_rows_sample.statement: Fixes the binding terminology register (from ratified FA-4): 'Zero' in prose means Zero(K,EC) (L2 function), other senses must be written as 'Z-KOS-001' (meta-principle) or 'the absence-lens Zero (2026-08-22)'; 'K_t/KnowledgeState' means the L2 formal state, other senses written as 'the complex-number K(t) model (ALT-09)' or 'the event-flow knowledge state (engineering usage)'; 'Kernel' must always be context-qualified (constitutional kernel/formal kernel candidate/historical formulations), bare 'kernel' forbidden in Part III; 'Committed' means the A6 decision-boundary status, colloquial use avoided entirely; 'Determination' means the Supported->Accepted transition, other sense written as 'the Tarka-era determination notion'; 'Lord' is history only, both readings named, forbidden in Part III; 'Atman/Atma-Kernel' means the unresolved lens (D-FA-5), forbidden as architecture; 'Omega' is a historical term decomposed per GN-09, written as Omega-a/Omega-b/Omega-c for the decomposition; Sanskrit terms carry their lens origin on first use per chapter.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A naming caution
a_rows_sample.statement: Warns the reader that K_t in the book always means the formal state; the discovery corpus also contains an earlier, unrelated K(t)=M(t)+iA(t) complex-number model of knowledge from five days before the formal era, and the engineering documents use 'knowledge state' for an event-flow record — three senses, one notation family, kept apart by the ratified terminology register.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Evidence map table
a_rows_sample.statement: Tabulates 9 claim-source-grade rows for III.3: I-7 X_t!=Observed(X_t) -> v0.2 invariants, Step 066 [FA]<-READ; Omega three-way decomposition -> semantic-lineage-map (dated revision), v0.2 GN-09 note [H]/[E]; Omega predates measure-theory era -> AF-003 (kernel docs 2026-08-24) [H]; K_t eight primitives -> v0.2 concept table (Steps 049/050) [FA]<-TESTED-within-scope; Step-050 audit 'not a proof' -> EXP-02 registry, corpus record [E]; K(t)=M(t)+iA(t) earlier sense -> ALT-09, 20260821-2325 [H]; event-flow 'knowledge state' -> 20260820-231930 (engineering usage) [H]; SourceObs!=SemanticObs -> v0.2 (125403 Option 3) [FA]<-READ, untested; Art. 6.5 observation!=inference -> Constitution v1.0 [E].

b_rows_sample.anchor: Zero != Lord != Sarathi != Transition ... K_t -Zero-> Z_t -Lord-> L_t -Sarathi-> a_t -Commit-> e_t -delta-> K_{t+1} ... Zero, Lord, and Sarathi do not change K
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the initial Zero/Lord/Sarathi/Commit/Transition pipeline as a linear sequence culminating in a state change, with explicit invariants that Zero, Lord and Sarathi are each analytical (never transformational) and none of their outputs alone entail K_{t+1}.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Sarathi should not 'recommend Commit'... Commitment is not an epistemic action. It is an authorization/governance action... a_t -Authorize-> c_t -Execute-> e_t. Guidance != Authorization != Execution != Transition.
b_rows_sample.statement: Removes 'Commit' from Sarathi's action vocabulary and inserts an explicit Authorization boundary between recommendation and execution: Sarathi produces a recommendation a_t, Authorize(Knower,a_t,Policy) produces a command c_t, Execute(c_t) produces an event e_t, and only then does delta(K_t,e_t) fire -- Guidance != Authorization != Execution != Transition, with the missing Authorize function explicitly making the Knower's authority mathematically visible.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Execute: C -> E is too deterministic. Execution can fail... Execute(c_t) -> ExecutionResult in {Success(e),Failure(f),Partial(e,f)} ... ExecutionResult != DomainEvent.
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects Execute from a total deterministic function C->E to one returning a structured ExecutionResult (Success/Failure/Partial), and similarly Authorize to return an AuthorizationResult (Authorized/Rejected/Deferred/Modified) rather than assuming every recommendation becomes a command; ExecutionResult is explicitly distinguished from the DomainEvent that actually triggers a transition.

b_rows_sample.anchor: the epistemic cycle is actually not always a cycle... External observation -> Event -> Transition can update the state directly... Guidance is optional; Transition is fundamental. G5 - Guidance is not a prerequisite for transition.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the closing theorem G5: Guidance (Zero/Lord/Sarathi) is not a prerequisite for every Knowledge-State transition -- a raw external observation event or a scheduled validity check can trigger delta(K_t,e_t) directly, so the lenses must never be modelled as mandatory middleware sitting between every event and the transition function; renames the pipeline from 'Epistemic Cycle' to 'Epistemic Guidance-and-Transition Cycle' to reflect this.

b_rows_sample.anchor: I strongly recommend introducing: I-hat_t = Candidate Ideal State and I_t = Approved Ideal State ... KnowledgeOS -> I-hat_{t+1} (proposal); Authorize(I-hat_{t+1}) -> I_{t+1}.
b_rows_sample.statement: Introduces a Candidate Ideal State (I-hat) vs Approved Ideal State (I) split mirroring the Q17 recommendation/authorization boundary: KnowledgeOS may only ever produce a candidate revision proposal, and only an explicit Authorize step (by the Knower/governance authority under applicable norms) produces the actually approved I_{t+1}; KnowledgeOS != I_{t+1} but KnowledgeOS -> I-hat_{t+1}.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Sārathi \rightarrow DecisionPosture
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects Sarathi's output from a binary Stop/Continue decision to a richer DecisionPosture ∈ {Proceed, Investigate, ProceedWithCaveats, Defer, Escalate, UnableToDecide}, argued to be closer to Sarathi's actual role.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Recommendation \neq Assertion
b_rows_sample.statement: Strict boundary: Recommendation ≠ Assertion, Recommendation ≠ Fact, Recommendation ≠ Decision. Sārathi may say 'Investigate the moral obligation dimension' but KnowledgeOS must not silently convert that into 'Therefore Arjuna should fight' — the Knower remains the decision authority unless the domain explicitly delegates that authority. Marked as extremely important for the DDD model.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Candidate \neq Knowledge
b_rows_sample.statement: Lord needs a stronger boundary too: Candidate ≠ Knowledge, Candidate ≠ Evidence, Candidate ≠ Assertion. A presentation should visually distinguish KNOWN / INFERRED / UNKNOWN / CANDIDATE / RECOMMENDED to prevent semantic contamination.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Zero(S_t) \rightarrow EpistemicFindings
b_rows_sample.statement: Reaffirms Zero's role as boundary-finder, not belief-decider: Zero(S_t) -> EpistemicFindings, Presentation ⊇ DecisionRelevant(EpistemicFindings); 'Zero does not decide what the Knower should believe. Zero says: Here is where the state has a boundary.' Also strengthens provenance: EveryDecisionRelevantClaim -> Provenance, with a worked claim-level provenance record example (Acquisition/Evidence/Observed-at/Validity/Conflict/Source).

b_rows_sample.anchor:
Unknown 
eq Absent 
eq NotApplicable 
eq NotObserved 
eq NotYetInvestigated
b_rows_sample.statement: Elevates 'unknown' to a fundamental principle already implicit in Zero: Unknown ≠ Absent ≠ NotApplicable ≠ NotObserved ≠ NotYetInvestigated, illustrated by Version=UNKNOWN not meaning Version=ABSENT, and SecurityStatus=NOT_ASSESSED not meaning SecurityStatus=SAFE.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Zero \neq UniversalValidator
b_rows_sample.statement: DDD warning that Zero risks becoming a 'god object' by owning detection of gaps, conflicts, type problems, temporal problems and epistemic boundaries all at once: Zero ≠ UniversalValidator. Zero is redefined narrowly as detecting epistemic boundaries/deficiencies relevant to current state and purpose, aggregating epistemic consequences of findings from separate domain validators (schema, type, policy, security violations).

b_rows_sample.anchor: LordCandidate \neq Knowledge
b_rows_sample.statement: LordCandidate ≠ Knowledge and LordCandidate ≠ Evidence: Lord can propose 'there may be a moral-obligation dimension' but it becomes knowledge only after investigation; critical to prevent AI-generated hypotheses entering the Knowledge State as facts.

b_rows_sample.anchor: S\bar{a}rathiRecommendation \neq Decision
b_rows_sample.statement: Sārathi needs a constitutional policy boundary: SārathiRecommendation ≠ Decision, SārathiAction ≠ HumanAuthorization — Sārathi may determine the next best investigation, but the Knower decides whether to accept it unless the system has explicitly delegated authority.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Sārathi: (K,U,N,\Delta,P,Role) \rightarrow Guidance
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects Sārathi(K,I,Δ)->Action as too simplistic: Sārathi:(K,U,N,Δ,P,Role) -> Guidance, which may then produce Decision, which may then authorize Action, giving Guidance ≠ Decision ≠ Action (confirming an earlier DDD warning). Also reframes Zero/Lord/Sārathi as three functions/lenses over the state rather than three sequential stages: Zero=Diagnose, Lord=Reason/Synthesize/Orient, Sārathi=Guide, with Decision->Action occurring outside those lenses; explicitly an architectural abstraction, not a literal theological equivalence.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Sārathi: (State, Norms, Role, Context, Discrepancies) \rightarrow Guidance
b_rows_sample.statement: Revises Sārathi(K,I,Δ)->Action (too direct) to Sārathi:(State,Norms,Role,Context,Discrepancies)->Guidance -> CandidateActions -> Decision -> Action, giving proper separation of concerns. Reaffirms Zero as a pure DiagnosticFunction that must not itself decide ('therefore do X'). Corrects Lord from 'merely a reasoning engine/LLM reasoning' to AuthoritativeKnowledge+NormativeOrientation+InterpretiveResolution, since Krishna in the text functions as an authoritative source of teaching, not just an inference engine — called crucial for KnowledgeOS governance. Confirms Sārathi = ContextualGuidance, distinguishing Lord ('what is authoritative/true/normative') from Sārathi ('how does that apply here') from Decision ('what will I choose') from Action ('what will I actually do').

b_rows_sample.anchor: Zero(K,I,C,P) \rightarrow \text{Epistemic Boundaries}
b_rows_sample.statement: Reframes Zero/Lord/Sārathi as product capabilities rather than domain entities: Zero(K,I,C,P)->Epistemic Boundaries acts as an 'epistemic diagnostic engine' (missing dimensions, unknown values, missing/weak/conflicting evidence, logical contradictions, stale knowledge, contextual mismatches, unresolved questions, unsupported assumptions, Ideal-State discrepancies); Lord asks 'what else might matter?' enabling 'horizon expansion' beyond gap-checking; Sārathi:(K,I,Z,L,Q,C)->NextAction performs 'epistemic navigation', worked through a Bhīṣma-relationship example (Zero flags unknown relationship, Lord flags kinship as material, Sārathi recommends investigating it before evaluating the decision).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Can we migrate this Nexus installation?
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked example: asked 'Can we migrate this Nexus installation?', a conventional AI answers directly, while KnowledgeOS first constructs required dimensions (version, repository inventory, blob stores, storage, network, DNS, firewall, certificates, backup, dependencies, authentication, operational constraints), runs Zero to find missing items (backup verification, firewall confirmation, certificate ownership, dependency inventory), and has Sārathi respond 'Do not decide migration readiness yet. Investigate these four items.'

b_rows_sample.anchor: perform justified action given epistemic state
b_rows_sample.statement: Contrasts a conventional agent optimizing 'complete task' against KnowledgeOS optimizing 'perform justified action given epistemic state', worked through a deploy-approval example: required knowledge checklist (code reviewed✓, tests passed✓, architecture approved✓, security assessment✗, production configuration✗, rollback strategy✗) yields Zero='3 critical gaps' and Sārathi='DO NOT DEPLOY. Investigate security, configuration and rollback.' Also frames the agent loop as Understand Intent->Construct Knowledge State->Discover Dimensions->Zero->Identify Gaps/Conflicts->Lord->Expand Possible Investigation->Sārathi->Select Next Epistemic Action->Agent/Tool->Observation->Update Knowledge State->Repeat, called 'an epistemically governed autonomous agent architecture'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Retrieve(Q,K_t,I_t,C) \rightarrow EvidenceCandidates
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects plain Retrieve(Query)->Documents to a goal-directed Retrieve(Q,K_t,I_t,C)->EvidenceCandidates: the retrieval system 'knows why it is retrieving', discovering relevant dimensions (e.g. version, repository topology, blob stores, firewall, certificates for a migration decision) before retrieving. Zero can drive retrieval: given a partially-filled knowledge-state checklist, Zero reports specific gaps (backup verification, firewall rules, certificate ownership) and Sārathi generates a concrete investigation plan (search infrastructure docs for backup configuration, etc.), giving Zero -> Gap -> Sārathi -> Retrieval as part of the investigation loop, not a one-shot lookup.

type_signature.domain: question x knowledge state x ideal state x context

b_rows_sample.anchor: \text{Zero}(K_t)\rightarrow\text{epistemic boundary}
b_rows_sample.statement: Zero continuously reveals 'what is still unknown' (Zero(K_t)->G_t, G_0->G_1->...); ideally G_t->∅, but if the knowledge space is genuinely unbounded Zero may never establish G_t=∅. The stronger concept is Zero(K_t)->epistemic boundary, with Moksha representing the boundary itself being transcended rather than merely all currently detected gaps being filled — judged 'much more profound'.

group_evidence.why_grouped: labels co-occur in the same contribution's labels[] 2 separate times across the corpus

a_rows_sample.anchor: We now move from 'can the problem be computed?' to 'can KnowledgeOS compute it reliably at organizational scale?' Correctness+Scalability+Predictable resource usage.
a_rows_sample.statement: Frames Step 90's shift from decidability to organizational-scale reliability, requiring Correctness+Scalability+Predictable resource usage.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 90.1 — Complexity is part of architecture ... T(n). O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2), O(2^n). Two mathematically correct algorithms can therefore have radically different engineering properties.
a_rows_sample.statement: States complexity T(n) is part of architecture: two mathematically correct algorithms can have radically different engineering properties depending on complexity class.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 90.2 — Experiment 1: linear growth ... n=1,000,000 knowledge objects. O(n). Expected: approximately proportional growth. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 1: an O(n) operation on 1,000,000 objects shows approximately proportional growth; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 90.3 — Experiment 2: quadratic growth ... O(n^2). n=1,000,000 gives ~10^12 comparisons. Expected: a mathematically valid algorithm may become operationally infeasible. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 2: an O(n²) pairwise-comparison operation on 1,000,000 objects (~10^12 comparisons) shows a mathematically valid algorithm can be operationally infeasible; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 90.4 — Knowledge graphs create combinatorial risk ... GraphSize ≠ ReasoningSize. The architecture must constrain the relevant reasoning subgraph.
a_rows_sample.statement: States GraphSize ≠ ReasoningSize: naive reasoning over a full knowledge graph G=(V,E) risks combinatorial explosion; the architecture must constrain the relevant reasoning subgraph.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 90.5 — Experiment 3: irrelevant graph explosion ... 10^7 entities. A decision concerns only 500. Expected: the reasoning engine should ideally operate on a relevant subgraph rather than the entire graph. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 3: a decision concerning only 500 of 10^7 entities should reason over a relevant subgraph, not the whole graph; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 90.6 — Relevance filtering ... G_Q⊆G, the query-relevant subgraph. Reason(Q)=Reason(G_Q). How do we know that G_Q contains everything necessary? This connects directly to Step 88's completeness problem.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the query-relevant subgraph G_Q⊆G with Reason(Q)=Reason(G_Q), raising the completeness question of whether G_Q contains everything necessary, explicitly linked to Step 88's completeness problem.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 90.7 — Experiment 4 ... Retriever reduces 10,000,000 objects to 1,000. But omits a mandatory governance rule. Expected: efficiency improved, but assurance failed. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 4: a retriever that improves efficiency (10M→1000 objects) but omits a mandatory governance rule shows efficiency improved while assurance failed; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 90.8 — Therefore optimization cannot precede assurance ... 'retrieve less information because it is faster' is wrong. First establish sufficient information; then optimize its processing.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the principle that optimization cannot precede assurance: information sufficiency must be established first, then processing can be optimized.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 90.9 — Incremental computation ... K_{t+1}=K_t+ΔK. ComputeIncremental(K_t,ΔK) instead of Compute(K_{t+1}).
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines incremental computation: ComputeIncremental(K_t,ΔK) is preferred over full recomputation Compute(K_{t+1}) when K_{t+1}=K_t+ΔK.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 90.10 — Experiment 5 ... 1,000,000 facts. One fact changes. Full recomputation costs 1000s. Incremental update costs 0.1s. Expected: incremental reasoning is preferable if semantic correctness is preserved. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 5: incremental update (0.1s) vastly outperforms full recomputation (1000s) for a single changed fact, preferable if semantic correctness is preserved; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 90.11 — Incremental reasoning requires dependency tracking ... A→B→C→D. If A changes, we must potentially invalidate B,C,D. DependencyGraph becomes computationally important.
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues incremental reasoning requires dependency tracking: a change to A in A→B→C→D may require invalidating B,C,D, making the DependencyGraph computationally important.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 90.12 — Experiment 6 ... Source E changes. Derived knowledge K_1,K_2,K_3 depends on E. Expected: K_1,K_2,K_3 become candidates for revalidation. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 6: a change to source E makes all dependent derived knowledge (K_1,K_2,K_3) candidates for revalidation; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 90.13 — Cache correctness ... cached knowledge has a validity interval ValidFrom/ValidUntil. A cache is therefore not merely a performance object. It can have epistemic semantics.
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues caches are not merely performance objects but carry epistemic semantics via a ValidFrom/ValidUntil validity interval.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 90.14 — Experiment 7 ... Policy changes at t_1. KnowledgeOS continues using cached policy P_old. Expected: StaleKnowledge. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 7: continuing to use a cached policy P_old after it changed at t_1 is StaleKnowledge; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 90.15 — Cache invalidation ... D=f(E,P,M). If E or P or M changes, D may no longer be valid. CacheValidity=f(InputVersion,PolicyVersion,ModelVersion).
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines CacheValidity=f(InputVersion,PolicyVersion,ModelVersion): a derived artifact D=f(E,P,M) may become invalid if any of E, P, or M changes.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 90.16 — Experiment 8 ... Risk calculation uses ModelVersion=4. Current model is ModelVersion=5. Expected: cached result must be recognized as derived under version 4. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 8: a cached result derived under ModelVersion=4 must be recognized as such even after the current model advances to version 5; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 90.17 — Parallelism ... Q=Q_1∪Q_2∪...∪Q_k. If Q_i are independent, they can be computed in parallel.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines decomposable reasoning tasks Q=Q_1∪...∪Q_k, parallelizable when the Q_i are independent.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 90.18 — Experiment 9 ... Five independent evidence checks each take 10s. Sequential: 50s. Parallel: ~10s. Expected: parallelization improves throughput. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 9: five independent 10s checks run in parallel take ~10s vs 50s sequential; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 90.19 — But dependencies constrain parallelism ... Q_3 depends on Q_1. Q_1→Q_3. They cannot simply be evaluated independently.
a_rows_sample.statement: Notes dependencies constrain parallelism: Q_3 depending on Q_1 (Q_1→Q_3) cannot be evaluated independently.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Steps 82-88 asked what can we know, infer, predict, aggregate, preserve. Step 89 asks what can actually be computed. Knowledge ≠ Computability ≠ Feasibility.
b_rows_sample.statement: Introduces Step 89's central distinction Knowledge ≠ Computability ≠ Feasibility: information can be True while Computability is False, or a computable answer may still be operationally infeasible.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.1 — Three different failures ... Case A Missing information: InformationInsufficient. Case B Undecidable: NoGeneralAlgorithm. Case C Computationally infeasible: algorithm exists but too expensive. Unknown, Undecidable, Intractable must not be represented as the same state.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines three distinct failure modes when a question cannot be answered: Case A InformationInsufficient (Unknown), Case B NoGeneralAlgorithm (Undecidable), Case C too-expensive-to-compute (Intractable) — none may be conflated.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.2 — Experiment 1 ... 'Was system X compliant?' KnowledgeOS has not retrieved the relevant policy. Expected: Unknown rather than False. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 1: a compliance question with unretrieved policy must yield Unknown, not False; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.3 — Experiment 2 ... Question is theoretically undecidable for arbitrary programs. KnowledgeOS fails to produce an answer. Expected: Undecidable rather than Unknown. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 2: a theoretically undecidable question must be labeled Undecidable, not merely Unknown; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.4 — Experiment 3 ... A problem has an algorithm but requires 2^100 operations. KnowledgeOS does not compute it. Expected: ComputationallyInfeasible rather than Undecidable. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 3: a decidable-but-2^100-operation problem must be labeled ComputationallyInfeasible, not Undecidable; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.5 — Decidability ... a decision problem is decidable if there exists an algorithm that accepts every valid input, terminates, and returns the correct answer. f:X→{0,1}, exists A such that A(x)=f(x) and T_A(x)<∞ for every valid x.
b_rows_sample.statement: Formally defines decidability: f:X→{0,1} is decidable if an algorithm A exists with A(x)=f(x) and finite runtime T_A(x) for every valid x.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.6 — Experiment 4 ... KnowledgeOS checks a finite set of explicit rules R_1..R_n. Each rule terminates. Expected: compliance checking is decidable for that formalized rule set. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 4: checking a finite set of terminating rules is decidable; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.7 — Finite-state systems ... S={s_1..s_n}. Transitions T⊆S×A×S. Questions such as 'can state s_bad ever be reached?' can often be solved algorithmically.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes reducing engineering governance questions to finite-state systems S with transitions T⊆S×A×S, enabling algorithmic reachability questions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.8 — Experiment 5 ... System has 100 finite states. A model checker evaluates all reachable states. Expected: Reachability is decidable. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 5: model-checking a 100-state system confirms reachability is decidable; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.9 — This is highly relevant to KnowledgeOS ... S_0-A_1->S_1-A_2->S_2. UnauthorizedDeployment ∉ ReachableStates could become a formal property.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes formalizing governance as explicit state transitions so that properties like UnauthorizedDeployment ∉ ReachableStates become formally verifiable.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.10 — Experiment 6 ... ApprovalRequired before ProductionDeployment. Formal transition model contains no transition Unapproved→Production. Expected: the model can formally establish that the transition is impossible within the model. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 6: a formal transition model lacking an Unapproved→Production transition formally establishes that transition is impossible within the model; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.11 — Important qualification ... Formal verification proves Property(Model)=True. It does not automatically prove Property(Reality)=True. If the model omits a bypass path, the proof may be irrelevant to reality.
b_rows_sample.statement: Warns that formal verification proves Property(Model)=True, not automatically Property(Reality)=True; a model omitting a real bypass path makes the proof irrelevant to reality.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.12 — Experiment 7 ... Formal model proves UnauthorizedDeployment=False. But a manually accessible production server exists outside the model. Expected: ModelCorrect but SystemAssuranceIncomplete. Result: PASS. This connects directly to Step 85's governance-surface concept.
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 7: a correct formal proof (UnauthorizedDeployment=False) alongside an out-of-model manual bypass server is ModelCorrect but SystemAssuranceIncomplete; result PASS; explicitly linked to Step 85/86's governance-surface concept.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.13 — Verification versus validation ... Verification: did we build the system according to its formal specification? Validation: does the specification/model actually represent the real system adequately? Both are necessary.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Verification (built according to formal spec) from Validation (spec adequately represents reality); both are necessary.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.14 — Experiment 8 ... Model is internally consistent but represents the wrong business process. Expected: Verification=True but Validation=False. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 8: an internally consistent model of the wrong business process shows Verification=True but Validation=False; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.15 — The halting problem ... Given arbitrary program P and input x, will P(x) eventually terminate? is undecidable in general. There is no algorithm H(P,x) that correctly answers this for all programs and always terminates.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the halting problem: no algorithm H(P,x) decides termination correctly for all programs and always terminates.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.16 — Experiment 9 ... 'Will every arbitrary program eventually terminate?' Expected: UndecidableInGeneral. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 9: the general termination question is UndecidableInGeneral; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.17 — Why this matters ... We should never design KnowledgeOS around the assumption EveryQuestion→DefinitiveAnswer. Some questions have NoGeneralAlgorithmicAnswer.
b_rows_sample.statement: Draws the design lesson: KnowledgeOS must never be designed around EveryQuestion→DefinitiveAnswer, since some questions have NoGeneralAlgorithmicAnswer.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.18 — But restricted domains can be decidable ... FiniteStatePrograms termination can often be decided. UndecidableGeneralProblem does not imply UndecidableEveryRestrictedInstance.
b_rows_sample.statement: States UndecidableGeneralProblem does not imply UndecidableEveryRestrictedInstance: restricting to finite-state programs can restore decidability of termination.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 89.19 — Experiment 10 ... General program termination: Undecidable. Finite-state workflow termination: Decidable. Expected: KnowledgeOS distinguishes the domains. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 10: KnowledgeOS must distinguish undecidable general-program termination from decidable finite-state workflow termination; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.statement: Candidate Theory-level methodological principle: a KnowledgeOS representation is not justified merely because it is semantically expressive; its reasoning consequences and computational tractability must be explicitly considered — an independent formal reason to resist building one universal semantic structure.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Expressiveness does not justify computational complexity by itself ... Semantic question: What distinctions can the representation express? Computational question: What reasoning can be performed over it, with what guarantees and cost? Neither question substitutes for the other.
b_rows_sample.statement: Methodological principle: expressiveness does not justify computational complexity by itself; every proposed KnowledgeOS semantic mechanism must separately answer a semantic question (what distinctions can it express) and a computational question (what reasoning can be performed, with what guarantees/cost) — neither substitutes for the other, grounded in KR&R's expressiveness/tractability tradeoff and reasoning-by-cases explosion.

b_rows_sample.anchor: There is a tradeoff between the expressiveness of a representation language and the difficulty of reasoning ... A slight increase in the expressiveness of a Description Logic may result in a drastic change in the complexity of reasoning.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Semantic expressiveness and computational tractability must be evaluated separately ... a_rows_sample.anchor: Do not put "critical thinking" into the KnowledgeOS kernel as a methodology. Extract the domain primitives that critical thinking requires.
a_rows_sample.statement: A critical-thinking practical guide (4 parts: critical thinking, logic/structuring/framing, problem solving, communication) is treated as a KnowledgeOS domain-analysis source, not a methodology to adopt; the rule is to extract domain primitives that critical thinking requires, not to encode critical-thinking methodology itself into the kernel.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS needs a Question
a_rows_sample.statement: The prior Observation->Evidence->Claim->Assessment model is missing a Question object; the SCQH pattern (Situation->Complication->Question->Hypothesis) shows the hypothesis is not the solution but an assumption/proposal used to investigate the question. Revised kernel flow proposed: Question->Inquiry->{Observation, Existing Knowledge}->Evidence->Hypothesis->Testing->{Support,Refutation}->Claim.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Question is not just a UI prompt
a_rows_sample.statement: Question is a DDD domain object with identity, subject, context, scope, purpose, origin, status, and possibly competing formulations (example Q-42: Context/Question/Purpose/Scope/Constraints), giving multiple agents a shared unit to work on -- a natural unit for KnowledgeOS collaboration.

a_rows_sample.anchor: An AI agent does not "create knowledge" directly. It participates in an Inquiry.
a_rows_sample.statement: Question (the epistemic object) is distinguished from Inquiry (the activity/process of investigating it, comprising search/observation/evidence collection/hypothesis formation/testing/assessment); an AI agent participates in an Inquiry rather than directly creating knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS can preserve not only what we concluded, but what we considered and rejected.
a_rows_sample.statement: Hypothesis (an assumption/proposal that predicts an answer and directs investigation, precise and subject to validation/disproof/refinement) must be first-class with fields HypothesisId/Proposition/Question/Context/Origin/Assumptions/ExpectedObservation/TestMethod/Status and lifecycle Proposed->UnderTest->Supported->{Refined,Rejected}, letting KnowledgeOS preserve what was considered and rejected, not only conclusions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeOS must preserve epistemic alternatives, not only accepted conclusions.
a_rows_sample.statement: RejectedHypothesis is itself knowledge: example of H1 (DNS)/H2 (firewall)/H3 (authentication) investigated for a Nexus failure, where testing yields H1 rejected, H2 supported, H3 unresolved -- a conventional repository would retain only the accepted conclusion, but KnowledgeOS should retain the reasoning history because rejected hypotheses are useful future knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: AI speculation must not automatically become knowledge.
a_rows_sample.statement: Hypothesis (a proposition currently being investigated) != Claim (a proposition being asserted/evaluated as knowledge); a Hypothesis tested via Assessment (supported/refuted/unresolved) may result in a KnowledgeClaim but not every hypothesis becomes a claim -- preventing the AI failure mode where speculation automatically becomes knowledge.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A claim inherits epistemic risk from unresolved assumptions on which it depends.
a_rows_sample.statement: Assumption is proposed as first-class (example: Architecture Claim 'Use deterministic asset URLs' depending on Assumptions A1-A3, so a change to A3 propagates an impact-detected signal to Claim C1); Assumptions need lifecycle semantics (Proposed/Accepted/Challenged/Validated/Invalidated/Superseded) and a candidate kernel invariant that a claim inherits epistemic risk from unresolved assumptions on which it depends.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Argument is another missing primitive
a_rows_sample.statement: Using the Paul-Elder reasoning-components framework (purpose, question/issue, assumptions, point of view, facts/information, concepts, inference/interpretation, implications/results), Argument is proposed as a structured reasoning object (Purpose/Question/Premises/Assumptions/Evidence/Inference/Conclusion/Implications/PointOfView) producing a Conclusion, replacing an undifferentiated 'AI text -> Claim' pipeline; not every claim is an argument.

a_rows_sample.anchor: the kernel should preserve how the conclusion was obtained
a_rows_sample.statement: Inference (moving from available information toward a conclusion, which can be wrong) should be an explicit first-class relation/process (Evidence+Assumption -> Inference -> Claim), different from merely saying 'C1 references E1 and E2' -- the kernel should preserve how the conclusion was obtained, aligning with deterministic replay and auditability goals.

a_rows_sample.anchor: do not add abductive reasoning based on this book. The source does not establish it in the retrieved material.
a_rows_sample.statement: Book distinguishes Induction (Observation->Pattern->Generalization->Hypothesis/Theory) from Deduction (Theory->Hypothesis->Test->Result, four-stage pipeline ending in possible disproof); ReasoningMethod should model Deductive/Inductive as an Inference.ReasoningMethod field rather than hard-coding them per domain object, but the author explicitly self-limits: do not add Abductive reasoning to the model because this source does not establish it.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Test should be distinguished from Verification
a_rows_sample.statement: Test ('an activity intended to produce evidence relevant to a hypothesis') is distinguished from Verification ('an assurance activity determining whether a defined condition or proposition satisfies an established criterion'); example: testing hypothesis 'Firewall blocks Nexus access' via curl differs semantically from verifying 'Port 443 is reachable from deployment subnet.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: Test refutes Hypothesis
a_rows_sample.statement: Refutation becomes a first-class event: the knowledge graph should support Evidence-supports/contradicts->Claim and Evidence-supports/refutes->Hypothesis, and Test-refutes->Hypothesis, not only 'Evidence supports Claim.'

a_rows_sample.anchor: I would not introduce a universal confidence score into the kernel.
a_rows_sample.statement: Assessment is enriched to Subject/Evidence/Assumptions/Inferences/ReasoningMethod/Tests/CounterEvidence/LogicalQuality/SourceQuality/Context/Time/Outcome, explicitly rejecting a universal 'confidence = 0.87' scalar.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Claim is an epistemic object. While ReasoningAssessment is an assessment of the reasoning used to establish it.
a_rows_sample.statement: Paul-Elder intellectual standards (Clarity/Accuracy/Precision/Relevance/Depth/Breadth/Logic/Significance/Fairness, presented on pages 21-22 as standards for evaluating reasoning) should form a ReasoningAssessment vocabulary kept separate from KnowledgeClaim itself, since Claim is an epistemic object while ReasoningAssessment assesses the reasoning used to establish it -- a clean DDD boundary; illustrated by a multi-dimensional assurance example replacing a single 'Claim = trusted' flag with separate Evidence/Reasoning/Assumptions/Source/Verification dimensions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Evidence is not intrinsically relevant. It is relevant to a Question in a Context.
a_rows_sample.statement: Relevance must be modeled as relational, not intrinsic: not evidence.relevance=true on the Evidence entity, but an EvidenceAssessment{evidence, question, relevance} record, since the same evidence can be relevant to Question Q1 but irrelevant to Question Q2.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 5W2H is a lens used to interrogate an Inquiry.
a_rows_sample.statement: The 5W2H framework (What/Where/When/Who/Why/How/How much) supports treating Context as non-optional metadata (What/Where/When/Who/Why/How/Magnitude), but should not become a literal FiveWTwoH entity -- instead it is a lens used to interrogate an Inquiry.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Problem probably belongs one level above the kernel
a_rows_sample.statement: Problem ('the gap between the current undesired state and desired state,' modeled as CurrentState/DesiredState/Gap/Impact/Context, feeding Problem->Question->Hypothesis->Investigation->Solution) is a useful concept but should NOT be a kernel primitive, since not all knowledge work (research, governance, documentation, AI reasoning) begins from a problem; it belongs to a Knowledge Work/Inquiry context concept layer, unlike Question/Hypothesis/Evidence/Claim/Argument/Inference/Assessment which are closer to kernel primitives.

a_rows_sample.anchor: MECE ... extremely useful for KnowledgeOS but not as a universal truth rule
a_rows_sample.statement: MECE (Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive) is not a universal truth rule but should become a DecompositionQuality / CoverageAssessment used to ask whether decomposition branches overlap or omit relevant items; Decomposition itself is proposed as a Question-decomposes-into-Question[] relation, preferred over implementing a dedicated IssueTree aggregate.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A decision uses knowledge. It does not itself become knowledge merely because it was made.
a_rows_sample.statement: Decision-making should remain separate from truth assessment: Knowledge != Decision; pipeline KnowledgeClaim->DecisionInput->Decision->Action keeps the epistemic kernel clean; a decision-matrix approach (Alternatives/Criteria/Weights/Scores/Result) is a perfect downstream consumer requiring a decision record to answer why it was made, which alternatives/criteria/evidence/assumptions were used, and who decided and when.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Question ≠ Inquiry. Inquiry { question, subject, authority context, purpose, evidence requested, response, resolution }.
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes Inquiry as a distinct kernel object (a Question is content; an Inquiry is an epistemic operation with its own schema), argued to fit well into the KnowledgeOS kernel.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Inquiry{inquiryId,question,subject,context,requester,authorityScope,evidenceRequirements,responses,determinations,status}. ChatMessage ≠ Inquiry — 'what is the Nexus architecture?' is communication, while 'determine whether Nexus conforms to approved architecture v1.1' has subject/purpose/evidence requirements/method/expected determination. AI conversation → Inquiry → Context → Agent Reasoning → Claims → Evidence → Determination; the conversation is not the authoritative artifact, the derived governed objects are.
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes Inquiry as a first-class domain concept, distinguishes it from a mere chat message, and shows how AI interaction becomes auditable by producing derived governed objects rather than treating the conversation itself as authoritative.

group_evidence.why_grouped: explicit agent-stated uncertainty: 'kos-inquiry-concept' POSSIBLY relates to 'critical-thinking-inquiry-lens' (batch B0025). Note: This batch's formalization of Inquiry as a distinct epistemic-operation kernel object (vs. Question as mere content), reprising and re-deriving a distinction already explored in the B0011/B0012 Inquiry lenses.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Detecting a contradiction != resolving a contradiction. KnowledgeOS must be able to detect and preserve unresolved conflict without inventing an answer
a_rows_sample.statement: States the central principle distinguishing contradiction detection from resolution.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_i. The organization therefore has mathcal K = {K_1,K_2,...,K_n}. There is no requirement that K_1=K_2
a_rows_sample.statement: Formally defines the multi-context knowledge collection with no equality requirement between contexts.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A in K_1 and B in K_2. We cannot immediately say A and B is contradictory. We first need semantic translation T_{1->*}(A) and T_{2->*}(B)
a_rows_sample.statement: Requires semantic translation before evaluating cross-context contradiction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Compatible(A,B,C). Possible values: {Compatible, Contradictory, Conditional, Unknown, NotApplicable}. This is preferable to a binary relation
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a graded five-value compatibility relation, preferable to binary contradiction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A genuine contradiction occurs when, under a common semantic interpretation and compatible conditions, A=>P and B=>not P. Then A perp B under the relevant context
a_rows_sample.statement: Formally defines genuine contradiction requiring common interpretation and compatible conditions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A perp B under C_1 but not under C_2. Therefore contradiction must carry Context
a_rows_sample.statement: States contradiction is itself contextual.

a_rows_sample.anchor: The service is available vs The service is unavailable ... Availability_Production and Availability_Test ... A not-perp B. The apparent contradiction was caused by missing context
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked production-vs-test availability example showing an apparent contradiction dissolved by context.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Before declaring contradiction, KnowledgeOS should attempt ContextResolution. This is another epistemic investigation
a_rows_sample.statement: Requires context disambiguation as an epistemic investigation prior to declaring contradiction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: ServerIP=10.61.133.85 at t_1. ServerIP=10.61.133.90 at t_2. These are not contradictory if t_1 != t_2 and the state changed. TemporalAlignment must precede contradiction detection
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked temporal-alignment example requiring time alignment prior to contradiction evaluation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A(t_1)=True and B(t_2)=True. This demonstrates Truth can be indexed by time
a_rows_sample.statement: States truth can be time-indexed, both statements can be simultaneously true at their respective times.

a_rows_sample.anchor: System supports TLS1.3 under Configuration=C_1. System does not support TLS1.3 under Configuration=C_2. the apparent contradiction disappears when conditions are represented
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked TLS-configuration example of conditional (non-genuine) contradiction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Align(A,B) = (Entity, Time, Context, Scope, Semantics, Conditions). Only after sufficient alignment should contradiction be evaluated
a_rows_sample.statement: Formally defines the six-dimension alignment required before contradiction evaluation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Claim A -> Context/Time/Entity/Scope/Semantics -> ALIGNMENT <- Claim B/Translation -> Compatibility Analysis -> Yes/No/Unknown -> OK/Conflict/Investigate
a_rows_sample.statement: Presents a contradiction-detection pipeline diagram.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Two contexts can conflict operationally without making logically contradictory statements ... DeployImmediately and DeployOnlyAfterApproval. These are conflicting prescriptions. But they are not necessarily factual contradictions
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes operational/normative conflict from factual contradiction, worked with a deployment-policy example.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Factual conflict: P versus not P. Semantic conflict: Same term, incompatible meanings. Normative conflict: Different rules prescribe incompatible actions. Conflict != Contradiction
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines three conflict classes (factual/semantic/normative) distinct from logical contradiction.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Rule_1: A->Action_1 and Rule_2: A->Action_2 where Action_1 != Action_2. Then there is a policy conflict
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes normative conflict as incompatible rule-prescribed actions.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Rule_A comes from ArchitectureBoard and Rule_B comes from ProjectTeam. They may have different authority levels. Authority(Source,Rule,Context) becomes relevant
a_rows_sample.statement: Introduces source-and-context-relative authority for resolving normative conflicts.

a_rows_sample.anchor: A senior authority can issue an incorrect factual statement. Authority != Truth. Authority determines what is binding, not necessarily what is factually true
a_rows_sample.statement: States the crucial distinction that authority determines bindingness, not truth.

a_rows_sample.anchor: TruthStatus and BindingStatus. TruthStatus=Unknown while BindingStatus=Mandatory. A governance rule may be mandatory even while its underlying assumptions remain uncertain
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes separate truth-status and binding-status dimensions for a claim.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Architecture Board mandates All production changes require approval. Even if someone argues that approval provides little technical value, the rule remains binding ... KnowledgeOS should represent Binding=True. It should not silently override the rule based on an optimization calculation
a_rows_sample.statement: Worked governance-mandate example warning against silently overriding binding rules via optimization.

b_rows_sample.anchor: When is there enough trustworthy knowledge to make a decision? This is different from asking whether a claim is true. A decision may depend on multiple independently necessary conditions
b_rows_sample.statement: Poses the central epistemic-sufficiency question, distinct from claim truth.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Sufficient(K,d) means that the available knowledge satisfies the epistemic conditions required by d. Sufficient(K,d_1) does not imply Sufficient(K,d_2)
b_rows_sample.statement: Formally defines decision-specific epistemic sufficiency, non-transferable across decisions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: P(SystemHealthy)=0.95. That might be sufficient for LowRiskPlanning. It may be completely insufficient for SafetyCriticalDeployment. EpistemicSufficiency is decision-specific
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked example establishing sufficiency is decision-specific, no universal threshold.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Pre(d) = {p_1,...,p_n}. Pre(d) = {IdentityConfirmed, CurrentStateKnown, SecurityValidated, GovernanceApproved}. The decision is admissible only if its required preconditions are satisfied
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines decision preconditions with a four-item worked example.

b_rows_sample.anchor: If p_1 is necessary: d=>p_1. But satisfying p_1 does not necessarily imply d. Necessary != Sufficient
b_rows_sample.statement: Formally distinguishes necessary from sufficient conditions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: SecurityValidated may be necessary. But it is not sufficient. We may also require TestingPassed, ArchitectureApproved, RollbackAvailable
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked production-deployment example of multiple necessary-but-not-individually-sufficient conditions.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A,B,C,D are mandatory. Then Sufficient(d) = A and B and C and D. This is the simplest assurance composition
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes conjunctive assurance composition.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A=True, B=True, C=False, D=True, then Sufficient=False. It does not matter that 75% of the conditions passed. For mandatory conditions, one missing condition can block the decision
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked weakest-link counterexample: 75% pass rate is still insufficient given one mandatory failure.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Assurance(A)=0.99, Assurance(B)=0.99, Assurance(C)=0.10. An average gives 0.693. That does not mean 69.3% safe. The low-assurance critical condition may be decisive
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked counterexample warning against averaging assurance scores, which masks a decisive low-assurance condition.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Criticality(p_i). But we should not simply multiply all probabilities together unless the probabilistic assumptions justify doing so. Mathematical composition requires semantic assumptions
b_rows_sample.statement: States criticality-weighted composition requires justified semantic assumptions, not blind multiplication.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Assurance = (Claim, Evidence, Method, Context, Time, Uncertainty, Validation, Scope). The scalar can be derived when appropriate
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines assurance as a structured eight-field object rather than a bare scalar.

b_rows_sample.anchor: EvidenceRequirement(d). Decision: Production Deployment. Required: Identity confirmed, Architecture approved, Security validated, Tests passed, Rollback demonstrated, Governance authorized. This is much closer to executable governance
b_rows_sample.statement: Presents a worked executable evidence-requirement specification for production deployment.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KS(K,d) in {True,False,Unknown}. Because sometimes we cannot establish whether the requirements are satisfied. Unknown must not silently become False or True
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines knowledge sufficiency as a three-valued predicate preventing Unknown from silently collapsing.

b_rows_sample.anchor: mathbb L_3 = {T,F,U}. T=established true; F=established false; U=unknown/undetermined. This is particularly useful for incomplete knowledge
b_rows_sample.statement: Formally defines three-valued epistemic logic L3.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A simplified three-valued conjunction: T/T=T, T/F=F, T/U=U, F/T=F, F/F=F, F/U=F, U/T=U, U/F=F, U/U=U. This is more appropriate than forcing missing knowledge into false
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the full three-valued conjunction truth table.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Similarly disjunction: T/T=T, T/F=T, T/U=T, F/T=T, F/F=F, F/U=U, U/T=T, U/F=U, U/U=U. This allows reasoning with incomplete information
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines the full three-valued disjunction truth table.

b_rows_sample.anchor: IdentityConfirmed=T, SecurityValidated=T, RollbackDemonstrated=U. Then Sufficient=False if rollback is mandatory, or Unknown if the policy itself does not establish whether rollback is mandatory
b_rows_sample.statement: Worked example applying three-valued conjunction to a concrete deployment decision.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Gate(d,K). Possible states: Pass, Fail, Blocked, Unknown
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a decision gate as a four-state predicate.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A gate can pass epistemically while the decision remains unauthorized. GatePass != Authorization. This reinforces Step 40
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes gate-pass from authorization, reinforcing Step 40's authority-vs-truth distinction.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Assurance(d) = Compose(A_1,A_2,A_3). But the composition rule must be explicit
b_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes assurance composition as requiring an explicit composition rule.

a_aliases: Cross-Context Consistency, Contradiction, Reconciliation and Epistemic Authority
b_aliases: Epistemic Sufficiency, Decision Preconditions, Assurance Composition and the Mathematics of Enough Knowledge
